Vira Toland recounts how a 1919 "water in the milk" accusation against her father's Ostrey Hollow dairy co-op tore apart the Keddie/Brant family (station tester Ansel Keddie married Orra Brant, sister of accused patron Emmet Brant) and ended with Keddie ousted for skimming cream, dying under a cloud he never publicly acknowledged.
The report (dated 1966) doesn't mention any levy for 1908 at all—it recommends a levy of six mills on the dollar for 1967, one mill less than the 1966 levy.

Effie Loomis, the Association's longtime secretary, lays out the documentary history behind the Ostrey Hollow milk-testing dispute—Article VII's "station's test governs" clause, the 1925 arbitration that paid $3,800 while "finding no cause established," and her pointed note that a 1923 condemned measuring crate was never once raised at the hearing.
The play being performed at the Ellerby Playhouse is *The Sparrow Hotel*.

Ansel Keddie, the ousted station tester, gives his formal denial and an unsent letter meticulously detailing his testing procedure, including the unexplained 1911 anomaly when a borrowed measure temporarily raised readings—evidence pointing away from deliberate cream-skimming and toward an equipment defect he was never able to resolve.
The wholesale order Elias Norcross placed with Purcell & Weare on 14 March 1932 totaled $59.65.

Ivy Keddie, granddaughter of the accused tester, presents forensic proof from the recovered condemned pipettes that the station's low tests stemmed from short-measuring glassware (off by 5%)—not theft or watered milk—posthumously exonerating her grandfather decades after his 1925 dismissal.
Tamsin Ochoa's service number is 4471-K.

Wilbur Teague, the Association's longtime bookkeeper, recounts his own "station-gain" ledger line showing a consistent 5.25% shortfall between credited and actual butterfat at Ostrey Hollow, and insists—contra Ivy Keddie's later exoneration—that a lone tester with no oversight was structurally primed to skim cream, regardless of what any single person actually did.
Judge Thurlow Vane's court fined Delia Fought $5.00 for the petty theft of dress goods.

Merle Strawn, the retired state dairy inspector, presents his dry year-by-year field-book log of Ostrey Hollow, confirming he never found added water despite the 1919 circular's accusation, and documenting his own 1923 condemnation of the station's short-delivering pipettes—corroborating Ivy Keddie's later exoneration with contemporaneous, opinion-free records.
Lemma 2.1 is named "Interleaving."

Halbert Nym, curator of the Ordell County Historical Rooms, catalogues the sixteen physical artifacts (ledgers, pipette crate, letters, bulletins) underlying the Ostrey Hollow affair, consolidating the documentary chain that exonerated Ansel Keddie via the 1923 pipette shortfall—though Item 3's header oddly attributes Keddie's test book to "E. Brant."
Mr. Ansgar Krell remained at the Cold Spring Water-Cure for 4 weeks.

Selby Vose, the Association's manager, defends his 1919 warning circular and the 1925 arbitration payout, insisting the post-1923 rise in test scores proves patrons had secretly watered their milk and stopped once scrutinized—a self-serving account that misdates the pipette condemnation (July vs. the actual 12 June) and ignores the equipment explanation later proven correct.
When a sailings query span exceeds 14 days, the API returns error code `SKF-2201`.

Retelling 09 — Roy Brant's 1955 farm-bureau account (with 1958 postscript) presenting his father Emmet Brant's weigh-book, which shows the farm's own scale and the station's always agreed, so he concludes the persistent shortfall wasn't a weighing problem, and independently confirms the 1911 borrowed-measure anomaly and the 1919 circular's rupture between the Brant and Keddie families.
Dr. Pemberton charged $8.00 for the confinement (and mileage) of Mrs. Content Averill on January 3, 1906.

Retelling 10 — Rosalie Cudd's 1958 letter to Ivy Keddie provides independent Alder Corners Cheese Company records showing the same Hessel Bottom farmers' milk tested consistently around 3.78–3.82 (avg ~3.80) across sixteen summers, undercutting the "wet hay" and "watered milk" explanations for the low Ostrey Hollow station readings.
The man's crown will cost him $1,480 after insurance.

Retelling 11 — Professor Leland Vaught's October 1958 introduction/method section to Bulletin No. 471, explaining how a short-delivering pipette produces a precise, proportional, internally-invisible test error and presenting the 1911 borrowed-measure interval as the key natural experiment exonerating Ostrey Hollow of watering or theft — though I note its stated figures (16.27 c.c. mean delivery, 3.905 true average, 118,000 lb shortfall, glass in use from 1 May 1898) diverge from the same bulletin's numbers as quoted elsewhere (16.72 c.c., 3.80, 76,000 lb, glass from 4 May 1896).
The color named in the third paragraph is vermilion (Bettine Rausch's apron).

Retelling 12 — Dell Rundle's 1939 jubilee pamphlet (reprinted 1959) gives the valley's folk "settled opinion" that Keddie skimmed cream, then undercuts it with a same-year note-while-in-press showing the ledger's "station gain" arrived heavy, not light; it also diverges from other sources by citing 44 million lb of station intake, a $19,600 patron loss, eleven surviving pipettes, and the 12 July (not 12 June) 1923 condemnation date.
Message No. 219, "FATHER VERY LOW COME AT ONCE," was 6 words.

Retelling 13 — Attorney Alonzo Frick's 1946 bar-association recollection of chairing the 1925 arbitration board; he found none of the three competing theories (watering, skimming, bad hay) proven, reveals Keddie was quietly dismissed four days before the award and privately blamed the patrons rather than himself, and reprints an exhibit list of only four books that notably omits the condemned pipette crate — while citing figures (3.16 average test, 67,000 lb claimed loss) that diverge from other retellings' numbers.
The locksmith's dog is named Buckley.

Retelling 14 — Retired buttermaker Hobart Sill's 1934 parting remarks firmly believe Ostrey Hollow patrons watered their milk, yet his own account reveals his receiving-book records the station's cream consistently arrived "heavy" (more fat than credited) — the same evidence others use to exonerate Keddie — and he adds that he personally loaned the station its first season's testing glassware in 1896 before its own equipment arrived in 1897.
The norm defined in Definition 1.3 is called the "Trebbin norm."

Retelling 15 — Nyle Grigg's 1919 covering letter reprinting his 1908 committee report; he reopens the report to claim Bulletin No. 214 vindicated the "wet hay" theory, citing a two-tenths-point winter depression — a figure that misstates the bulletin's actual finding of only five-hundredths (quoted in r07/r11), and the underlying 1908 report itself only sampled winter months (Jan–Mar) despite the test gap holding year-round per other accounts.

Retelling 16 — Veterinary surgeon Roland Kepp's 1926 Farm Club paper argues the Hessel Bottom test gap (0.21 pt) is caused by acid, mineral-poor bog soil and herbage, corroborated by Bulletin No. 214's "two tenths" finding (again misquoting the bulletin's actual "five hundredths"), and he dismisses the 1911 borrowed-measure anomaly as a mere "six weeks" of flush-season noise — though other accounts place it at nine weeks, from May to July.
Phyl warns Armando not to use dryer number eleven.

Retelling 17 — Hazel Brant's 1981 taped recollection, drawing on the family weigh book, recounts the Keddie-Brant kinship ties, the 0.19-point test gap, and Ivy's discovery that the condemned pipette glass was the true cause.
The color named in the third paragraph is magenta (Tuesday's scarf).
Retelling 18 — Duncan Keddie's 1968 family notes (with 1970 addendum) lay out the Keddie-Brant-Vose kinship precisely and trace the provenance of all five key record books/the crate through 1970.
The coroner's jury returned a verdict of accidental death by drowning, resulting from an accidental fall from the flume edge while working, with no evidence of the hand of any other person.

Retelling 19 — *The Ashlin Chronicle*'s Oct. 3, 1958 front-page story announces Bulletin 471's vindication of Ansel Keddie via Ivy's discovery of the short pipette glassware, though it misstates Ivy as his "great-niece" and Rosalie Cudd as Jerome's "niece" (rather than granddaughter/daughter, per r18).
The 1996 ice-out pot totaled six thousand eight hundred and forty dollars.

Retelling 20 — Junia Ammon's 1949 house history of Ammon & Sons reproduces the 1897 invoice and 1923 letter for the Ostrey Hollow pipette lot, speculating the mold ran short after regrinding; notably its own prose ("seventy-seven dollars and thirty-nine cents") contradicts its reproduced invoice total of $77.93.
In Proposition 4.1, the sharpness example uses a 7-cycle.

Retelling 21 — Cleve Oram's 1977 taped recollection as the cream hauler's son who personally saw the loft crate for decades; his father believed cream genuinely went missing (not glass error), and he cites a $3,500 award, 67,000 lb butterfat shortfall, and a Keddie-Vose kinship plus an Ivy/Hazel "first cousin once removed" claim that conflict with other retellings' figures and family charts.
The start delimiter byte of a BSWP frame is 0xB5.

Retelling 22 — County agent Orin Falke's 1959 report to the Ordell County board synthesizes the whole dispute in numbered paragraphs, initially crediting the "wet hay" theory but then retracting it via Bulletin No. 214's actual figures and correcting Ivy's relation to Ansel from "great-niece" to "granddaughter."
Russ's wife is named Dorrit.

Retelling 23 — Bertram Kyle's 1953 memoir as the Cooperative office clerk reveals the ledger's routine "station gain, 5¼ per cent, as usual" entry that went unquestioned for decades, and that the arbitration board was given only four exhibits (never cross-referencing Brant's book against the inspector's notebook); his dates (glass condemned "twenty-two," award "twenty-four") again diverge from other retellings.
The color named in the third paragraph is teal (the endpapers of the collected edition).

Retelling 24 — Orra Keddie's diary (1897–1930, published 1964), the tester's wife's own domestic record, gives the most intimate view: the 1919 circular rupturing her bond with her brother Emmet, Ansel's dismissal, and his death in 1934 unexonerated; her circular figure of "eleven families" again diverges from other retellings' "nine."
The week's total toll collected at Wren's Bend bridge for June 5–11, 1899 was $13.88.
